props.title: All.I.Can.

sections.content: **All.I.Can. (2010)** (2010) revolutionized ski cinematography by blending environmental messaging with breathtaking action sports footage. Created by Sherpas Cinema, it arrived when ski films like **That's It, That's All** (2008) and The Art of Flight (2011) were pushing visual boundaries. But All.I.Can. went further, using innovative time-lapse photography and creative urban skiing sequences to highlight humanity's impact on mountain environments. The famous JP Auclair street segment in Trail, BC became instantly iconic, influencing action sports filmmaking for years to come.

sections.content: The environmental themes in **All.I.Can.** sparked a new wave of conscious action sports filmmaking. Chasing Ice (2012) used stunning glacier photography to document climate change, while **Days of My Youth** (2014) balanced spectacular skiing with meditation on nature's fragility. These films moved beyond pure action porn to tackle bigger questions about outdoor recreation's relationship with the environment.

The technical innovation in **All.I.Can.** deserves special attention. Director Dave Mossop pioneered new camera techniques, including mounting high-speed Phantom cameras on helicopters. This influenced later films like McConkey (2013) and **View From A Blue Moon** (2015), which pushed camera technology even further. The film's creative urban segments also inspired a generation of street skiing videos, proving that creative vision could trump big budgets. SUBHEAD: Impact on Action Sports Filmmaking

sections.content: The marriage of artistry and athleticism in **All.I.Can.** changed how action sports stories are told. **The Fourth Phase** (2016) adopted similar environmental themes while following snowboarder Travis Rice, and **La Liste** (2016) used comparable techniques to capture extreme skiing. The film proved that action sports documentaries could be both visually spectacular and intellectually engaging.
